core.text: Attack the routine dependency on bulk acknowledgment of registered pending identities. Failed account: dashboard-pending identities are uniformly outstanding recognition demand, so immediate bulk advances every recipient. N1 is already recognized but remains pending through boundary 3. Bulk at tick 0 enqueues N1 before N2; tick 1 therefore consumes a duplicate slot. This refutes the account, not every possible bulk schedule.

Surviving valued function: eight independent registrations and eight distinct sender recognitions. Preserve registration as request eligibility. Fresh builder should construct selective early requests and later batching from these limits: individual N2 at tick 0 bypasses N1; bulk remains available after its display clears. Removing bulk entirely requires seven new individual requests and exceeds six actions.

Builder limits: six successful one-tick registrations remain; seven new recognitions remain. Empty initial queue makes tick 0 unusable for delivery, leaving eight slots for seven first successes. Requests become eligible next boundary; tick 8 requests cannot help. Dispatcher has six actions, one per tick; roles cannot exchange. FIFO processes one entry per tick, including failures and duplicates. Schedule N8 delivery at ticks 6-8. No added capacity or altered timing is available.

residue.text: Closest rival: immediate default bulk, with identical registration choices. Separating probe: analytically trace two stipulated starts, requesting bulk versus individual N2 at tick 0, then idle dispatch at tick 1. Compare boundary-2 queue and recognition ledgers. Bulk predicts duplicate N1 at tick 1 and one total recognition; individual predicts N2 success and two. Defeat of the selective account would be no such ledger difference under these rules, or a later proposed completion exceeding six actions or boundary 9.

Displaced work: dispatcher must choose identities and request boundaries rather than blindly repeat bulk; every selection still spends an action. Registrar retains six validations. Server retains seven necessary first deliveries, while wasted entries consume scarce slots. Ledgers are readable without added clerk labor. A fresh builder must tabulate registrations, request actions, eligible queue entries and first recognitions; this handoff establishes no completed execution.
Delay origin is unknown. Later sender adaptation and extra demand are unobserved hypotheses and cannot justify present scheduling. No empirical comparison or globally best schedule proof is supplied.
